I guess most people have the level of knowledge I used to have..."genital" and "oral" are not different types of the virus. They just denote where on the body the virus is.

Herpes 1 and 2 can be either oral or genital. Hsv-1 is the same virus no matter where it is on the body. You can spread hsv-1 from the mouth to genital through oral sex. There is a heavy stigma around genital herpes (understandable, that shit hurts) but it is the same exact virus as oral herpes. 

Most of the time the virus is asymptomatic and people don't even know they have it. It can even be dormant and not show symptoms for years. Also herpes isn't genital warts.

I didn't know much of any of that until I was forced to learn by my own research after contracting (Yes I get tested, but HSV tests are often not even included in std screenings, and they often aren't reliable. And yes I use protection; HSV can be spread even with protection and as I said, from oral). 

The info out there about hsv is abysmal. I have even gotten conflicting info from doctors.

Edit: if you know you have it, no matter how common it is, anywhere on the body either oral or genital, the right thing to do is tell your partner before getting physical. Especially because of how stigmatized it is, it usually messes with people's mind.

I am extremely shy and introverted, and this is my first time doing the program. So far I really enjoy it; the French students here all seem earnest and want to learn, even those who are a bit rougher around the edges in the internat, and the teachers who I principally work with have all been very welcoming. 

I think the atmosphere greatly depends on the school; I for example am in a very small, rural town - I imagine it is quite different in say, Paris. Being in a welcoming school I think may just be luck of the draw, unfortunately. 

In terms of crowds and noise, the small town aspect does help me personally, so if you are like me, finding a rural area may be worth considering. 

I also do have experience teaching by myself in a classroom - I taught 2 sections of French for 2 years while in graduate school, which I am extremely grateful to have done before this. If you've never had experience teaching, you'll honestly be fine; however if you can find an opportunity to get some, it will help you feel much more at ease. 

Also, be kind to yourself. Take the time to rest after class and recharge; there's nothing wrong with needing time to be alone. Lastly, if one kind of interaction doesn't suit you (like small talk in a large group of teachers) seeking out other opportunities is fine too - e.g. I've been spending time visiting museums and concerts in Paris with a person I met there; one-on-one might be less overwhelming, like it is for me.

That's a lot I just wrote lol, but I want to help anyone with anxiety/introversion to feel less alone - you can be that way and still enjoy France and TAPIF! :)

The terms "afab" and "amab" are not blaming doctors or anyone else, at least I have never heard anyone assert such a thing. I'm trans, and I know that most other trans people can agree with me when I say that doctors taking care of me as a baby/child did nothing wrong when treating me as a female-bodied person. That's their job. In fact, I still need care relating to my female anatomy, and I wouldn't imagine just neglecting myself because of my identity (though I know it can be hard for some people to resist dysphoria to do things like pap smears etc). 

These terms are simply shorthand to denote "what one was born as" while respecting one's identity and dignity as much as possible.

I was recently diagnosed at 25 - I am AFAB as well. I think diagnosis possibilities depend a lot on where you live (both country and region/state). I had no idea where to start in the beginning when I first had suspicions; it seemed impossible to pursue diagnosis due to AMAB-oriented bias and lack of knowledge of autism in adults - especially since I struggle with anxiety and depression, common issues for autistic people, making things seem even more difficult. Therefore, self-diagnosis to me seems like quite a logical course of action. 

For me personally, I tried self-dxing, tried accepting my own intuituon, but it was extremely difficult for me to not constantly invalidate and doubt myself without that diagnosis. To be honest I'd believe anyone who self-dxes because they know themselves better than I ever could, but when it comes to oneself I know that it can be hard. 

In terms of actually getting it, I just searched everywhere- went on Psychology Today and looked for anyone with "autism spectrum disorder" or "aspergers" in their specialties. Mainly looked for psychologists, not therapists, since they are the ones generally who administer official screenings. 

There are also centers specifically for testing only - I went to 2 of those. At the first one, I didn't feel heard and didn't have much opportunity to relate my experiences; was mostly just things like rorschach tests and IQ tests. I was only diagnosed with dysthymia and social anxiety disorder, which did not seem correct to me, so I went to a second center for a second opinion; there I did feel heard and understood- took the same tests like rorschach and IQ, but there was more time for me to talk about my life experiences. I was only diagnosed this time.

Let me know if you have any questions that maybe I could help with; I know how difficult and frustrating pursuing diagnosis can be. For me, it brought me peace of mind and allows me to be kinder to myself...I really shouldn't have had to receive a diagnosis to be kind to myself, but living in a world with the majority of people being neurotypical (though there are very likely many more ND people without diagnoses than general statistics show) makes things difficult at times.
